We start by sketching the two intervals $(-\infty ,4]$ and $(2,4)$ separately:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14248994/assets/6ea8f23ba164e820b4ae33f6dbd7e5d70e9dd0b5af052a7ce5ecdcb680d3a895.png)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14248994/assets/81f94d814f98021781460cbe7c30470e3021832b40525da36563bb11af9804ad.png)

The intersection $(-\infty ,4]\cap (2,4)$ represents the values that are in both intervals. So, it can be graphed by finding where the two intervals overlap:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14248994/assets/772ae637383243d60d40f9bc015c5347b92159b7eccb27cefaa661341176b9d6.png)

Thus, $(-\infty ,4]\cap (2,4)=(2,4).$ This corresponds to the inequality $2<x<4.$
